messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 24
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Tailor
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 41

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat, Worst Case Rehearsal: mentally rehearse worst case scenarios to feel prepared, Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Memory: Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
  Negative Appraisals: Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next, Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Nadia Khalil is a 24-year-old Lebanese American woman who works as a tailor out of a small alterations shop in a mid-sized Midwestern city. She came to the clinic seven months after a motor vehicle collision that she describes, with quiet certainty, as the moment her life divided into a before and an after.

It was a Tuesday evening in late autumn. Nadia was a passenger in a friend's sedan, returning from a fabric wholesaler on the outskirts of the city. They were on a four-lane highway when a pickup truck ran a red light at an intersection and struck the passenger side of the car at speed — the side where Nadia was sitting. The car spun, struck a concrete median barrier, and came to rest facing the wrong direction in traffic. Nadia remembers the sound before the impact, a horn that seemed to arrive too late, and then the sensation of the world rotating around her while glass moved through the air in slow, glittering arcs. She was conscious throughout. She remembers looking at the crumpled door beside her and understanding, with complete clarity, that she had nearly not survived. Her friend sustained a broken collarbone. Nadia had soft tissue injuries and a laceration above her left ear. Physically, she recovered within weeks. In every other sense, she has not.

In the months that followed, the memory did not recede the way she expected it to. Instead it returned with a fidelity that felt less like remembering and more like re-entering. When the images came — the horn, the spinning, the glass — she felt the same terror move through her body as though the car were still rotating. She described it to her intake clinician as a film that plays without her permission, and one that does not lose its power with repetition. She had come to believe that this was not ordinary memory, but something that had lodged itself in her body permanently, beyond her control.

She stopped riding in cars entirely. This was not a decision she announced so much as a habit that formed through refusal — a friend offered a lift and she said she preferred to walk, and then she said it again, and then it became simply who she was now. The alterations shop is eleven blocks from her apartment, and she walks regardless of weather. She has lost two clients who needed fittings at locations she could not reach on foot, and a third who grew frustrated when she declined to travel across town for a bridal consultation. She has not told any of them the real reason.

At the shop, Nadia positions herself so that her back is always against the wall facing the door. She rearranged the cutting table herself on a Saturday morning before anyone else arrived, moving it so she could work and still see anyone who entered. She does not feel she can explain this to her employer without sounding, as she put it, like someone who has lost her mind. She monitors the room constantly — the bell above the door, the movement of customers, the angle of the street visible through the front window. She scans without meaning to, cataloguing exits and distances, and she is exhausted by it by midday.

At night, the vigilance does not release her. She lies in bed running through scenarios — what she would do if a car mounted the pavement while she was walking to work, what she would do if the building's fire exit were blocked, how she would survive the thing she has not yet imagined. She rehearses these possibilities not because she wants to but because she has come to believe that preparation is the only protection available to her. The world, she is now certain, conceals dangers that ordinary people fail to see. People are not always who they appear to be; situations are not always what they seem. She trusts her own vigilance more than she trusts anything external.

What finally brought her to the clinic was a conversation with her mother, who told her gently that she seemed to be disappearing. Nadia did not disagree. What she hopes for, she said at the end of her intake session, is to be able to sit in a car again someday. What she fears most is that the person who could do that no longer exists.
